questions.stem: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in the 1910s. Why did most geologists reject his idea at the time?
options: He relied only on the shapes of coastlines and offered no other evidence
He could not give an acceptable mechanism to move the continents
He had no fossil evidence that linked the southern continents
He argued that the continents had always been in their present positions
questions.explanation: Wegener gathered fossil, rock and climate evidence, but the forces he suggested were far too weak to push continents through the ocean floor, so most geologists rejected drift. The mechanism came decades later with seafloor spreading and plate tectonics.

questions.stem: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small reptile of shallow coastal and inland waters, are found in southern Africa and eastern South America. How did Wegener use this?
options: As evidence that a land bridge sank into the ocean
As evidence that the reptile evolved twice, separately
As evidence that the two continents were once joined
As evidence that the reptile swam across the Atlantic
questions.explanation: A small reptile of shallow waters could not have crossed a wide, deep ocean, so its distribution is best explained by Africa and South America having been joined. Sunken land bridges were the rival explanation of the time, which Wegener argued against.

questions.stem: Glacial deposits and scratched bedrock about 300 million years old are found in India, Africa and Australia, now in warm latitudes. Which conclusion did Wegener draw?
options: These regions were once joined near the South Pole and have since moved
The whole Earth was covered in ice, including the regions at the equator
The glaciers flowed uphill across the oceans from Antarctica to each region
The deposits were formed by rivers and were mistaken for glacial features
questions.explanation: Matching glacial evidence across continents now far apart and in warm climates is explained if they were joined in Gondwana near the South Pole and later drifted. At the same time, the northern continents were forming tropical coal swamps, which rules out a global ice cover.

questions.stem: Why does the fit between South America and Africa match best along the edges of the continental shelves rather than the present coastlines?
options: The shelves were added after the continents separated
The coastlines have been built out by volcanic activity
The shelf edges mark the true edges of the continents
The coastlines were moved by the opening of the ocean
questions.explanation: Continental shelves are submerged parts of the continents, so their edges are the real boundaries of the continental crust. Coastlines change with sea level and erosion, so they give a poorer fit.

questions.stem: Marie Tharp plotted echo-sounding depth data from the Atlantic Ocean floor in the 1950s. What did she find along the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
options: A smooth, flat plain of thick ocean sediment
A line of old granite mountains like the Alps
A deep rift valley running along its length
A chain of deep trenches beside volcanic arcs
questions.explanation: Tharp's profiles showed a valley running down the ridge crest, which she interpreted as a rift where the crust was being pulled apart. Earthquake epicentres were later found to follow the same valley. Trenches occur at convergent boundaries, not on ridges.

questions.stem: How did Tharp's map of the ocean floor strengthen the case for continental drift?
options: A rift along the ridge showed the ocean floor was splitting apart
Trenches beside the continents showed they were sinking into the mantle
Thick sediment on the ridge showed the ocean floor was extremely old
Granite in the ridge showed it had once been joined to the continents
questions.explanation: A rift valley is a sign of tension, so a rift following the ridge suggested the crust was being pulled apart there, giving a place where new ocean floor could form. Sediment on ridge crests is thin, not thick, because the crust there is young.

questions.stem: What drives convection currents in the mantle?
options: The Earth's spin throws hot rock outwards and pulls cold rock in towards the poles
Tides raised by the Moon squeeze the mantle, making hot rock flow towards the surface
The magnetic field drags molten rock around the core in a continuous circular path
Heat from below makes rock less dense and rise, and gravity pulls cooler, denser rock down
questions.explanation: Heat from the core and from radioactive decay warms the base of the mantle, so that rock expands, becomes less dense and slowly rises. Cooler rock near the top is denser and sinks under gravity. Heat and gravity together keep the circulation going.

questions.stem: In a laboratory model, a crystal of potassium permanganate is placed at one side of a beaker of water, which is heated under that side. What does the coloured water show?
options: Warm water sinking directly above the heat source and rising on the opposite side
Warm water rising above the heat, spreading across the top and sinking as it cools
Cool water rising above the heat and sinking near the opposite side of the beaker
Coloured water spreading evenly in all directions from the crystal by diffusion only
questions.explanation: Water heated from below expands, becomes less dense and rises, then spreads across the surface, cools, becomes denser and sinks, forming a convection cell. The dye shows this loop. Diffusion alone would be far slower and would not form a circulating pattern.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the mantle with the water in a convection model?
options: The mantle is rigid and cannot flow, so convection in it is only a theoretical idea
The mantle is solid rock that flows extremely slowly, while the water flows freely
The mantle is a liquid like water, so it circulates at a similar speed to the model
The mantle is heated from above by the Sun, while the water is heated from below
questions.explanation: Mantle rock is solid but, over millions of years at high temperature, it deforms and flows by centimetres per year. Water in the model is a liquid that circulates in seconds, so the model shows the pattern but not the material or the timescale.

questions.stem: How does the age of ocean floor rocks change with distance from a mid-ocean ridge?
options: It is the same everywhere across the whole ocean basin
It increases on one side and decreases on the other
It increases with distance on both sides of the ridge
It decreases with distance on both sides of the ridge
questions.explanation: New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides, so rock is youngest at the ridge and progressively older towards the edges of the ocean. This symmetric pattern is key evidence for seafloor spreading.

questions.stem: The oldest ocean floor is less than about 200 million years old, while some continental rocks are about 4 billion years old. What does this show?
options: Ocean floor is constantly created and destroyed, while continental crust survives
The oceans formed long after the continents, about 200 million years ago
Continental crust is denser than oceanic crust, so it lasts much longer
Ocean floor rocks wear away quickly in water, so the older rocks have dissolved
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is recycled: it forms at ridges and is subducted back into the mantle at trenches, so none is very old. Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct easily, so it survives. The oceans themselves are far older than the present ocean floor.

questions.stem: As basaltic lava cools at a mid-ocean ridge, what records the direction of the Earth's magnetic field at that time?
options: Cracks in the rock that open in the direction of the field as it cools
Magnetic minerals in the lava that line up with the field as the rock cools
Layers of sediment that settle on the lava in the direction of the field
Bubbles of gas in the lava that stretch out in the direction of the field
questions.explanation: Iron-bearing minerals such as magnetite align with the Earth's magnetic field while the rock is hot, and the alignment is locked in as the rock cools. This preserves a record of the field's polarity when the crust formed.

questions.stem: Surveys show stripes of normal and reversed magnetic polarity in the ocean floor. Why is their pattern strong evidence for seafloor spreading?
options: The stripes are found only on the continents beside the ocean
The stripes are all of normal polarity near the ocean's edges
The stripes form a mirror image on either side of the ridge
The stripes run at right angles to the ridge across the ocean
questions.explanation: If crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides while the field reverses, each band of rock should be matched by an identical band on the other side. The symmetric stripes, interpreted this way in the 1960s, matched this prediction. The stripes run parallel to the ridge, not across it.

questions.stem: The boundary between two magnetic stripes lies 40 km from a ridge axis on each side and records a reversal 2 million years ago. What is the full spreading rate of the ridge?
options: 4 cm per year
2 cm per year
20 cm per year
0.4 cm per year
questions.explanation: Each side moved 40 km = 4,000,000 cm in 2,000,000 years, which is 2 cm per year. The plates move apart from each other at twice this, 4 cm per year. Giving 2 cm per year is the half rate for one side only.

questions.stem: According to the theory of seafloor spreading, where is new oceanic crust formed?
options: At ocean trenches
At hotspot volcanoes
At transform faults
At mid-ocean ridges
questions.explanation: Magma rises beneath mid-ocean ridges and solidifies to form new oceanic crust, which then moves away from the ridge on both sides. Oceanic crust is destroyed at trenches, where it is subducted.

questions.stem: If new crust is constantly made at ridges, why is the Earth not growing larger?
options: New crust is denser, so the Earth stays the same size as it slowly shrinks
The ridges add material only to the continents, which are then eroded away
Crust made at the ridges melts back into the mantle beneath the ridge itself
Old oceanic crust is destroyed at the same rate by subduction at trenches
questions.explanation: Harry Hess proposed that oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle at deep-sea trenches. Creation at ridges is balanced by destruction at subduction zones, so the Earth's surface area stays about the same.

questions.stem: How does seafloor spreading relate to the movement of tectonic plates?
options: The continents plough through the ocean floor while the ocean floor itself stays still
Spreading moves only the ocean floor, and the continents stay fixed above the mantle
The plates move only at transform faults, and spreading affects only the oceans
The ocean floor is part of the plates, so spreading carries the plates and their continents
questions.explanation: Continents are not pushed through the ocean floor, as Wegener thought. Both are parts of rigid lithospheric plates, so as new ocean floor forms at a ridge, the whole plate, including any continent on it, moves away from the ridge.

questions.stem: Why do hotspot volcanoes form a chain of volcanoes that get older in one direction?
options: The plume of hot mantle moves under a fixed plate, leaving a line of new volcanoes
The volcanoes are pushed apart from each other by the eruption of new magma
The oldest volcanoes formed first at the edge of the plate and the others followed
The plate moves over a fixed plume of hot mantle, carrying each volcano away from it
questions.explanation: A hotspot plume stays roughly fixed in the mantle while the plate above it moves, so each volcano is carried away from the plume and becomes extinct while a new one forms above it. The age trend shows the direction of plate motion.

questions.stem: In the Hawaiian chain, the active volcanoes are at the south-east end and the islands get older to the north-west. In which direction is the Pacific Plate moving?
options: South-west
North-west
South-east
North-east
questions.explanation: The youngest volcanoes sit over the hotspot, and older ones have been carried away from it in the direction of plate motion. Since they get older to the north-west, the plate is moving north-west over the hotspot.

questions.stem: An extinct volcano in a hotspot chain is 300 km from the active hotspot and is 4 million years old. What is the average plate velocity?
options: 1.3 cm per year
0.75 cm per year
7.5 cm per year
75 cm per year
questions.explanation: 300 km = 30,000,000 cm, and 30,000,000 cm / 4,000,000 years = 7.5 cm per year. Dividing age by distance gives about 1.3, and a slip in converting kilometres to centimetres gives a power-of-ten error.

questions.stem: The Cosgrove hotspot track in eastern Australia runs about 2,000 km, from volcanoes about 33 million years old near Townsville to about 9 million years old near Melbourne. What average plate speed does this give?
options: About 6 cm per year northward
About 8 cm per year northward
About 6 cm per year southward
About 8 cm per year southward
questions.explanation: The track records 2,000 km of motion over 33 - 9 = 24 million years: 200,000,000 cm / 24,000,000 years is about 8 cm per year. The volcanoes get younger to the south, so the plate moved north over the hotspot. Using 33 million years alone gives about 6 cm per year.

questions.stem: What is slab pull?
options: The drag of mantle flow on the base of a plate that carries it along like a conveyor
The pull of the Moon's gravity on a plate that moves it slowly around the planet
The pull of a cold, dense subducting slab that drags the rest of its plate behind it
The push of new crust at a ridge that forces the rest of the plate away from the ridge
questions.explanation: Old oceanic lithosphere becomes colder and denser than the mantle beneath, so once it starts to subduct, its weight pulls the rest of the plate towards the trench. The push from an elevated ridge is ridge push.

questions.stem: What causes ridge push?
options: Earthquakes at the ridge shake the plates and shift them sideways
Seawater cools the ridge and contracts it, pulling the plates inwards
Elevated, hot lithosphere at a ridge slides down and away under gravity
Magma injected at the ridge forces the plates apart like a wedge
questions.explanation: Lithosphere at a ridge is hot and stands high. As it moves away it cools and thickens, so the plate slopes down from the ridge and gravity causes it to slide away. It is a gravitational effect, not magma forcing the plates apart.

questions.stem: Plates attached to long subducting slabs, such as the Pacific Plate, move several times faster than plates with little subducting slab, such as the Eurasian Plate. What does this suggest?
options: Slab pull contributes more to plate velocity than ridge push or basal drag
Ridge push contributes more to plate velocity than slab pull or basal drag
Basal drag is the only force that changes the velocity of a plate
Plate velocity depends mainly on how much continent a plate carries
questions.explanation: The strong link between having a subducting slab and moving fast suggests slab pull is the largest driving force. Ridge push contributes less, and basal drag can help or resist motion depending on how the mantle moves relative to the plate.

questions.stem: Basal drag can act in either direction. When does it resist a plate's motion?
options: When the plate is attached to a long, dense subducting slab
When the mantle beneath flows faster in the plate's direction
When the plate carries no continental crust at all
When the plate moves faster than the mantle flowing beneath it
questions.explanation: Basal drag is friction-like coupling between the plate and the mantle below. If the mantle flows faster in the same direction, it drags the plate along; if the plate moves faster than the mantle, the mantle holds it back.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates how the evidence for plate tectonics developed?
options: A single discovery of magnetic stripes proved plate tectonics without needing any other evidence
Wegener's continental drift was accepted unchanged once the shape of the coastlines was mapped
The theory relies only on models in laboratories, because plate motion has never been measured
Separate lines of evidence, from fossils to sea-floor magnetism, combined to support one theory
questions.explanation: Plate tectonics was accepted because independent evidence agreed: fossil and rock matches, sea-floor mapping, sea-floor ages, magnetic stripes and earthquake patterns. Plate motion is now also measured directly with GPS, so it is not based only on models.

questions.stem: How can maps of earthquake and volcano locations be used to find active plate boundaries?
options: Earthquakes and volcanoes occur evenly across the middle of every plate
Volcanoes mark plate boundaries, but earthquakes occur only inside plates
Earthquakes and volcanoes occur mostly on the oldest parts of continents
Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur in narrow belts along plate boundaries
questions.explanation: Plates interact at their edges, so most earthquakes and volcanoes are concentrated in narrow belts that outline the plates, such as the ring around the Pacific. A few occur inside plates, for example over hotspots.

questions.stem: A boundary has many shallow earthquakes, no volcanoes, and rock offset sideways along a fault. What type of boundary is it?
options: A divergent boundary
An ocean-continent boundary
An ocean-ocean boundary
A transform boundary
questions.explanation: At transform boundaries plates slide past each other, producing shallow earthquakes and horizontal offsets but almost no volcanic activity, since no magma is created. Divergent and subduction boundaries both have volcanoes.

questions.stem: Which feature is an example of a continental transform boundary?
options: The Alpine Fault in New Zealand
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge in Iceland
The East African Rift Valley
The Himalayas in southern Asia
questions.explanation: The Alpine Fault runs along the South Island where the Australian and Pacific Plates slide past each other. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge and East African Rift are divergent, and the Himalayas formed at a continental collision.

questions.stem: On a sea-floor map, short fault lines cut across a mid-ocean ridge at right angles and offset it into segments. What are these faults?
options: Oceanic transform faults
Ocean-ocean subduction zones
Continental rift valleys
Fold and thrust belts
questions.explanation: Mid-ocean ridges are broken into segments by transform faults where the plates on either side slide past each other. They are oceanic transform boundaries, with shallow earthquakes along the active section between the ridge segments.

questions.stem: Which features would show a continental divergent boundary on a geological map?
options: A belt of folded and thrust-faulted rock forming high mountain ranges
A long fault offsetting rivers sideways, with no volcanoes nearby
A rift valley with normal faults, shallow earthquakes and basalt volcanoes
A deep trench beside a chain of explosive volcanoes on the continent
questions.explanation: Where a continent is pulled apart, blocks drop down along normal faults to form a rift valley, as in East Africa, with shallow earthquakes and mainly basaltic volcanism. Trenches mark subduction, fold belts mark collision and offset rivers mark transform faults.

questions.stem: At an ocean-continent convergent boundary, why does the oceanic plate subduct beneath the continental plate?
options: Oceanic lithosphere is thicker than continental lithosphere
Continental lithosphere is hotter and is being pushed downwards
Continental lithosphere is denser than oceanic lithosphere
Oceanic lithosphere is denser than continental lithosphere
questions.explanation: Basaltic oceanic lithosphere is denser than granitic continental lithosphere, so it sinks beneath it into the mantle. Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct far, which is why it survives for billions of years.

questions.stem: At an ocean-continent subduction zone, earthquake foci get deeper with distance inland from the trench. What does this pattern show?
options: The subducting slab slopes down into the mantle beneath the continent
The continental plate is sinking beneath the oceanic plate at an angle
Magma is rising from the core towards the trench through the mantle
The plates are sliding past each other horizontally along the coast
questions.explanation: Earthquakes occur within and along the cold, brittle subducting slab, so their foci trace a zone sloping down from the trench beneath the continent, reaching depths of hundreds of kilometres. Only subduction zones produce such deep earthquakes.

questions.stem: Volcanic arcs form above subduction zones, some distance inland from the trench. What mainly causes the melting that supplies them?
options: Pressure from the colliding plates squeezes solid rock until it turns directly into magma
Water released from the sinking slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge above it
Friction between the plates at the trench heats the rocks until the whole slab melts
The slab sinks into the outer core, which melts it and sends magma back to the surface
questions.explanation: As the slab descends, heat and pressure drive water out of its minerals. The water rises into the hot mantle wedge above and lowers its melting point, so it partly melts. Friction at the trench is not enough to melt the slab, and slabs do not reach the outer core intact.

questions.stem: Two oceanic plates converge. Which features form, as in the Mariana Islands?
options: A mid-ocean ridge and a central rift valley
A fold mountain range with no volcanoes at all
A transform fault with a line of hotspot islands
A deep ocean trench and a volcanic island arc
questions.explanation: When two oceanic plates converge, the older, denser one subducts, forming a trench. Melting above the slab feeds volcanoes that build a curved chain of islands, a volcanic island arc, on the overriding plate.

questions.stem: Why do continent-continent collisions, such as the one forming the Himalayas, produce high mountains but little volcanic activity?
options: Neither continent is dense enough to subduct deeply, so crust thickens instead of melting
Both continents subduct together, so all of their magma solidifies deep in the mantle
The continents slide past each other sideways, so no crust is compressed or melted
The collision zone is under the ocean, so water cools any magma before it can erupt
questions.explanation: Continental crust is buoyant, so neither plate subducts far. The crust is compressed, folded and stacked by thrust faults, thickening it into high ranges. With little subduction, little magma is produced.

questions.stem: Which type of fault forms where crust is pulled apart by tension?
options: A thrust fault
A strike-slip fault
A normal fault
A reverse fault
questions.explanation: Tension stretches the crust, and the hanging wall slides down relative to the footwall along a normal fault. Reverse and thrust faults form under compression, and strike-slip faults under shear.

questions.stem: A force diagram shows two arrows pointing towards each other across a fault, and the hanging wall has moved up relative to the footwall. What fault and boundary does it represent?
options: A reverse fault, typical of a convergent boundary
A normal fault, typical of a divergent boundary
A strike-slip fault, typical of a transform boundary
A normal fault, typical of a convergent boundary
questions.explanation: Arrows pointing together show compression, which pushes the hanging wall up over the footwall, forming a reverse fault; low-angle ones are thrust faults. These are typical of convergent boundaries. A normal fault forms under tension, with the hanging wall moving down.

questions.stem: In a sandbox model, a student pushes two blocks of layered sand past each other horizontally in opposite directions. Which fault does this model?
options: A strike-slip fault, as at a transform boundary
A normal fault, as at a divergent boundary
A reverse fault, as at a convergent boundary
A thrust fault, as in a fold mountain belt
questions.explanation: Opposite horizontal movement is shear, which produces strike-slip faults with mainly sideways displacement, as along the San Andreas or Alpine Faults. Normal faults need tension and reverse or thrust faults need compression.
